papers.title: Mas receptor activation promotes mitophagy and preserves neuronal function after traumatic brain injury.
papers.summary: This paper investigates how activation of the Mas receptor, part of the renin-angiotensin system's protective arm, influences mitochondrial quality control after traumatic brain injury (TBI). The researchers found that stimulating this receptor enhances mitophagy, the selective clearance of damaged mitochondria, in neurons following injury. This process appears to protect neurons from dysfunction and death, suggesting Mas receptor activation could be a therapeutic strategy for TBI.
papers.why: This directly relates to the core focus on mitophagy in neurons and offers a potential pharmacological angle for future mitophagy imaging or spatial omics studies in injury models.

papers.title: NAD<sup>+</sup> modulates REST isoform expression and its downstream mitophagy in Alzheimer's disease.
papers.summary: This paper investigates how NAD+ (a key cellular energy and signaling molecule) influences the expression of different isoforms of REST, a transcription factor involved in neuroprotection, in the context of Alzheimer's disease. It shows that NAD+ levels affect how REST isoforms regulate mitophagy, the process of clearing damaged mitochondria. The findings suggest that boosting NAD+ could restore proper mitophagy and REST function, potentially offering a therapeutic angle for Alzheimer's disease.
papers.why: This directly connects to the project's focus on mitophagy in neurons and its regulation by metabolic factors, relevant to understanding neurodegeneration in brain circuits.
papers.figure: A figure showing NAD+ levels correlated with REST isoform expression and mitophagy markers across control vs Alzheimer's disease brain tissue.

papers.title: Retinal ganglion cell autophagy: a housekeeper essential for neuronal homeostasis and survival.
papers.summary: This paper reviews how autophagy acts as a critical housekeeping mechanism in retinal ganglion cells, clearing damaged proteins and organelles to maintain cellular health. It discusses how disruptions in this process can compromise neuronal homeostasis and lead to cell death, which is relevant in diseases like glaucoma. The abstract frames autophagy as essential for long-term survival of these specific central nervous system neurons.
papers.why: Since retinal ganglion cells are projection neurons of the central nervous system, insights into their autophagy-mediated neuronal homeostasis can inform parallel mechanisms of mitophagy and autophagy dysfunction being studied in brain interneurons.

papers.title: Mitochondrial quality control in health and disease: mechanisms and therapeutic targets.
papers.summary: This paper reviews how cells maintain healthy mitochondria through quality control mechanisms like mitophagy, mitochondrial biogenesis, fission/fusion dynamics, and protein quality surveillance. It discusses how failures in these processes contribute to various diseases, particularly neurodegenerative conditions where damaged mitochondria accumulate. The review likely also covers emerging therapeutic strategies that target these quality control pathways to treat disease.
papers.why: Since the abstract is generic without a specific figure to highlight, understanding core mitophagy and mitochondrial quality control mechanisms provides essential mechanistic background for interpreting neuronal mitophagy patterns in spatial transcriptomic and metabolomic datasets.

papers.title: FLCN loss is characterized by SQSTM1/p62 accumulation despite functional autophagy flux in Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome-associated kidney cancer.
papers.summary: This paper studies Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome-associated kidney cancer, which is caused by loss of the FLCN gene. The researchers found that cells lacking FLCN accumulate the protein SQSTM1/p62, which is often used as a marker for blocked autophagy. However, despite this accumulation, their experiments show that autophagy flux (the actual degradation process) remains functional, suggesting p62 buildup is not simply due to autophagy failure.
papers.why: This paper is relevant because it clarifies a common pitfall in interpreting SQSTM1/p62 accumulation as a proxy for autophagy flux, a methodological issue directly applicable to studying mitophagy/autophagy dynamics in neurons and interneurons.

papers.title: New insights on microglial lysosomal acidification: A therapeutic target of neurodegenerative diseases.
papers.summary: This paper reviews how microglia—the brain's immune cells—use lysosomal acidification to properly digest cellular debris and dysfunctional organelles. When this acidification process fails, it impairs microglial waste clearance and is linked to the buildup of toxic proteins seen in neurodegenerative diseases. The authors propose that restoring proper lysosomal pH in microglia could be a promising therapeutic strategy for these conditions.
papers.why: Since microglial lysosomal/autophagic function directly parallels the neuronal mitophagy and autophagy pathways central to this PhD project, understanding shared degradation mechanisms across brain cell types could inform interpretation of spatial transcriptomic/metabolomic data on organelle clearance defects in neurons and their surrounding niche.

papers.title: FOXO3 Counteracts Oxidative Stress-Induced Nucleus Pulposus Cell Senescence via BNIP3-Mediated Mitophagy in Intervertebral Disc Degeneration.
papers.summary: This paper studies intervertebral disc cells (nucleus pulposus cells) and how oxidative stress causes them to become senescent, contributing to disc degeneration. The researchers found that a protein called FOXO3 helps protect these cells by activating BNIP3, a protein that promotes mitophagy (selective clearance of damaged mitochondria). By boosting mitophagy through this pathway, FOXO3 reduces oxidative damage and delays cellular senescence, offering a potential therapeutic target for disc degeneration.
papers.why: Although this study focuses on spinal disc cells rather than neurons, the core molecular mechanism—FOXO3-BNIP3 mediated mitophagy in response to oxidative stress—is directly relevant background for understanding mitophagy pathways that may also operate in neuronal health and interneuron resilience.

papers.title: Cytostatic autophagy: an underappreciated form of autophagy and its ramifications in cancer.
papers.summary: This paper discusses a form of autophagy that stops cells from dividing (cytostatic autophagy) rather than promoting cell death or survival. It explores how this autophagy variant influences cancer biology, potentially affecting tumor growth and treatment responses. The abstract likely reviews mechanisms and implications for therapy without providing new experimental image or spatial data.
papers.why: While centered on cancer, this review could offer conceptual insight into autophagy's non-degradative regulatory roles that may inform interpretation of mitophagy/autophagy states in neurons beyond simple clearance functions.
